newsitem.title: GERMANY: Reconnaissance jets join hunt for kidnapped German.
newsitem.headline: Reconnaissance jets join hunt for kidnapped German.

text.p: Two German Tornado jet fighters equipped with heat-seeking devices and cameras scanned a wooded area on Friday in the search for a kidnapped Frankfurt multi-millionaire.

Frankfurt prosecutor Rainer Schilling said police were tipped off about the area west of Frankfurt after one of two detained suspects told investigators they had taken Jakub Fiszman there two weeks ago.

The reconnaissance planes covered some 32 square km (12 sq mile) of the Taunus region about 50 km (30 miles) from Frankfurt where around 500 police continued to search for Fiszman, missing for over two weeks.
The air force jets criss-crossed the area in some 20 sorties, flying at only 200 metres (600 feet) above ground at more than 750 km (450 miles) per hour, German military officials said.

Investigators said they were becoming more pessimistic about finding Fiszman alive. His brother Georg paid a ransom of four million marks ($2.6 million) on October 10, but his kidnappers reneged on an agreement and failed to free him the following day.

The 40-year-old businessman, whose family's fortune has been put at Over 400 million marks ($260 million) and is best known for financing the failed Frankfurt production of the rock musical "Tommy", was last heard from when he called a friend on October 2.
"We have no concrete evidence that he is dead but we are more pessimistic than we were yesterday," police spokesman Ulrich Petri said at the scene of the search.
Police said the two suspects in custody are 48-year-old Rainer Koerppen and his 26-year-old son, Sven. Three other people detained in the probe were released on Friday.
Schilling said Sven Koerppen had confessed to police that he and his father took Fiszman on October 4 to the area now being searched by police.

Schilling said the son told police he and his father waited for Fiszman outside his office on the night of October 1 and took him to his father's house in a Frankfurt suburb, where he was held until October 4.
Before entering the wooded area, Rainer Koerppen made his son get out of the car and then drove off with Fiszman before returning about 30 to 45 minutes later alone.
"The son said his father wanted to take Fiszman to an area where he would not be able to escape," Schilling told Reuters.
A news blackout on the kidnapping was lifted last weekend in the hope that the public could helping to find Fiszman.
Police recovered most of the ransom on Wednesday in the garden of an apartment in Wiesbaden owned by Koerppen's parents.
Schilling said police were reviewing whether there was any connection between the abduction of Fiszman and that of his nephew in 1991.
The nephew, who was six years old at the time, was released three days after he was kidnapped. Media reports have said the family paid one million marks ransom after he was released.

The Hesse state police director, Juergen Noeckel, said at the weekend there were certain details in a letter from the kidnappers in the abduction of Fiszman that could only have been known to the 1991 kidnappers. ($1=1.5423 Mark)
